name: onnxruntime

facts.description: ONNX Runtime: cross-platform, high performance ML inferencing and training accelerator

title: ONNX Runtime: A Cross-Platform Inference and Training Engine for AI Models
answer: ONNX Runtime is Microsoft's open source, cross-platform engine for running and training machine learning models, released under the MIT licence and written mainly in C++. It sits at the inference and serving layer of the AI stack, executing models exported in the ONNX format across CPUs, GPUs and NPUs. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its performance advantages depend heavily on execution providers and model optimization, so the same model can behave very differently across hardware targets.

sections.body: ONNX Runtime is made by Microsoft and published as an open source project under the MIT licence, with its repository at microsoft/onnxruntime and its official site at onnxruntime.ai. The site describes it as a cross-platform, high performance machine learning inferencing and training accelerator, and the repository lists C++ as its language. It occupies the runtime layer of the AI stack, the part that takes a trained model and executes it efficiently on a chosen piece of hardware. Models arrive in the ONNX format, an open and portable representation, and ONNX Runtime turns them into running inference or training jobs. The project is actively maintained, with a last push recorded in October 2026 and roughly twenty two thousand stars on GitHub, and it is not archived. Its role is therefore not to define model architectures or to replace training frameworks, but to be the execution and serving substrate beneath them, spanning cloud servers, desktops, browsers, mobile devices and embedded accelerators.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The site presents ONNX Runtime as doing inference first and training second. On the inference side it runs large language models, vision models and small on-device models, with blog posts covering DeepSeek, Phi-2, Mistral, CodeLlama, Orca-2, Gemma, LLaMA-2, Stable Diffusion Turbo and SDXL Turbo, and it reports accelerating over 130,000 open source models from Hugging Face. It supports float32, float16 and int4 precision, and its execution providers target CPUs, CUDA GPUs, NPUs and browser runtimes such as WebGPU and WebAssembly. On the training side, ORT training is available through the torch-ort package as part of the Azure Container for PyTorch, and it accelerates training through optimized kernels and memory optimizations while remaining composable with DeepSpeed and Megatron. It is strongest where a model must run on many kinds of hardware, where latency and memory matter, and where the same artifact needs to reach cloud, desktop, web and mobile targets. The Goodnotes case shows this pattern in practice, a single in-house LSTM model deployed on-device to Windows, Web and Android with no internet connection required.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve depends on how deep you go. Running a model through the Python package is approachable for someone who already knows basic machine learning workflow, since the conversion and inference APIs are ordinary Python calls. Going further requires systems knowledge, because execution providers, quantization formats, build configurations and reduced size builds all involve hardware and packaging decisions. The ORT format documentation assumes familiarity with ONNX models, build configuration files and platform constraints, and the Vitis AI page expects developers to install vendor software such as Ryzen AI Software and to understand INT8 and BF16 quantization. Mathematics is not the main barrier, but an understanding of model graphs, precision and memory helps considerably. For a beginner, the official site offers documentation, blog posts and tutorials, though much of the material is written for developers who already have a model and a target device in mind rather than for someone starting from nothing.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around ONNX Runtime is broad and largely organized around the ONNX format and execution providers. The site documents providers for AMD Vitis AI, NNAPI, CoreML, CUDA, WebGPU, WebNN and WebAssembly, among others, and shows integrations with PyTorch through torch-ort, with Hugging Face models, and with optimization tools such as Olive. Olive is described as a state-of-the-art model optimization toolkit for the ONNX runtime, and it supports quantization algorithms including AWQ and GPTQ, fine-tuning with LoRA, and a shared cache backed by Azure Storage so teams can reuse intermediate models. The documentation covers model conversion, performance tuning, quantization and reduced size builds, and the blog publishes regular engineering case studies. Community support appears through the GitHub repository, which carries a substantial star count and ongoing commits, and through the wider ONNX and PyTorch ecosystems. The site does not present a formal certification or training programme, so learning is mostly documentation led.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: ONNX Runtime is built for both quick experiments and demanding production, but the two paths look different. Prototyping is fast because a model can be exported to ONNX and run through the Python package with little code, and the Goodnotes team reported that its prototype demonstrated simple integration. Production use is where the engineering effort appears, since performance comes from choosing execution providers, quantizing to float16 or int4, and converting models to the ORT format for size-constrained environments such as mobile and web. The site reports large gains in this configuration, including up to 7.39x faster prompt throughput than PyTorch Compile for Phi-2, up to 20.48x improved performance with int4 quantization compared to PyTorch, and 20x to 550x speedups for browser background removal with WebGPU and WebAssembly. The cost is complexity. Compilation for accelerators such as the Ryzen AI NPU can take minutes before the first inference, and optimization choices such as Fixed versus Runtime style must match the target provider.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site shows adoption across consumer software, mobile and cloud. Goodnotes used it to bring a scribble-to-erase feature from iPad to Windows, Web and Android, and the blog describes work with Arm KleidiAI, AMD Ryzen AI, NVIDIA TensorRT, Hugging Face and Azure. Microsoft maintains the project and integrates it with its own PyTorch container offering, which suggests it is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, at least for cross-platform inference. For someone choosing what to learn, this matters because the skills transfer across hardware vendors and deployment targets, and because the same runtime appears in browser, mobile and data centre contexts. The facts and the site do not provide adoption numbers, salary data or a list of employers, so any claim about the size of the job market would go beyond what is documented here. What can be said is that the project is actively developed and widely referenced in vendor documentation.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: ONNX Runtime is typically used alongside, not instead of, the major training frameworks. PyTorch models are exported to ONNX and then executed by ONNX Runtime, and the torch-ort package lets training code be wrapped with the ORTModule API after only a few lines of change. TensorFlow and PyTorch models can both be quantized through the Vitis AI Quantizer, and Olive accepts models from these ecosystems for optimization. The polyglot pattern is therefore a training framework in Python producing an ONNX artifact, an optimization step through Olive or a vendor quantizer, and a deployment step through ONNX Runtime on whatever hardware is available, whether that is a CUDA GPU, an NPU, a browser through WebGPU, or a mobile package using the ORT format. The site also positions it against other inference paths, comparing it with torch.compile and Llama.cpp in its benchmarks, which places it in the same layer as those runtimes rather than above or below them.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The main limits are complexity and uneven coverage. Performance depends on execution providers, and the site notes that some are experimental, such as Olive support in the Vitis AI provider, while others require vendor software to be installed first. Compilation for accelerators can take minutes and must finish before the first inference, which is awkward for rapid iteration. The ORT format is only supported from version 1.5.2 onward, and conversion requires a matching Python package version, so version drift is a real concern. The site does not say how many models fail to convert cleanly, how large the community is in absolute terms, or how the project is governed. It also does not state licensing or support terms beyond the MIT licence in the repository facts, and it offers no direct comparison of total cost against alternative serving stacks. Those questions remain open in the material reviewed.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
